definition: Irrevocable means incapable of being taken back or withdrawn.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word irrevocable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know irrevocable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The dean was plain about expulsion: the decision is irrevocable, reopened by no appeal, apology, or later good conduct.
An offhand promise is barely fastened — either side can shrug it away; irrevocable is fastened forever.
A binding deal must be honored, yet lawyers dissolve binding deals every week by mutual consent; irrevocable goes further — no consent, court, or regret can take it back.

Final says the matter is closed and nothing comes after it — a final score, a final answer. It stays silent about whether anyone could reopen it. Irrevocable speaks to exactly that question: the maker of the act cannot take it back, however much regret arrives later.

Permanent describes how long something lasts — a state meant to continue indefinitely, like a permanent stain or a permanent post. Irrevocable describes an act of will the maker cannot recall: a vow, a bid, a ruling. A permanent arrangement might still be revoked someday; an irrevocable one never can be.

Before the first lot, the auctioneer gives the room its one warning: 'A raised paddle is an irrevocable bid.' Wave at a friend, stretch, change your mind while your arm is still in the air — the bid stands, and the vase is yours.
Nothing you say afterward reaches back to unmake the offer you made.
Irrevocable is the precise word because it targets the taking-back: a commitment its own maker cannot recall.
Final says only that nothing came after; binding says you must honor it while it stands.
Irrevocable welds the escape hatch shut — there is no 'on second thought' with any power to act.
Irrevocable belongs to acts of will — gifts, vows, bids, rulings — and says the maker cannot take them back.
Its unit-mate irreversible belongs to processes and damage: you revoke a promise but reverse a trend.
If the thing that can't be undone is something someone did on purpose, irrevocable is usually the truer word.

Every fall, counselors walk seniors through the fine print of early-decision applications.
Most of an application stays soft until spring: essays can be swapped, majors changed, financial forms amended.
The early-decision pledge is different.
Sign it, and your acceptance — if it comes — commits you; the agreement is irrevocable from the moment of your signature, not from the school's reply.
Counselors stress what the word does and doesn't cover.
It doesn't mean forever — students transfer out of colleges every year.
It means the signer cannot take the promise back.
Regret in March changes nothing you set in motion in November.
